W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS

Clinical Genomics for Bioinformatics

Author

Eunji Ha

Published

June 2, 2026

Why GWAS belongs in this course

GWAS is directly clinical

  • Drug target validation — targets with human genetic support are ~2× more likely to succeed to approval [Reay & Cairns 2021]
  • Disease subtyping — same diagnosis, different genetic architecture → different biology & treatment
  • Risk stratification — polygenic risk scores in preventive medicine (W3)
  • Shared aetiology — genetic correlation quantifies overlap between diseases
  • Causal inference — Mendelian randomization tests causality without an RCT

▶️ Open a recent Nature Medicine paper — there’s a good chance GWAS data sits underneath the clinical claim.

What a GWAS actually asks

“Which genetic variants are more common in people with disease X than in matched people without it?”

  • Compares allele frequencies at millions of variants at once
  • Hypothesis-free — agnostic to which gene matters
  • Output is a list of associated loci, not causal genes (yet)
SNP (single-nucleotide polymorphism)

a single base-pair position where two or more alleles occur commonly (MAF ≥1%).

Humans carry ~10 million common SNPs; arrays measure 0.5–5M directly and impute the rest.

Genetic architecture: the shape of the signal

Know your trait before you run anything

Genetic architecture = the landscape of genetic contributions: how many variants, how large their effects, how frequent they are, and how they interact [Timpson 2017].

Architecture Variants Example Tools
Monogenic one phenylketonuria, CF (CFTR) family, WES/WGS
Oligogenic few some lipid traits targeted seq
Polygenic many, small height, T2D large GWAS
Omnigenic ~all expressed genes most complex traits huge GWAS + networks

The omnigenic model: regulatory networks are so interconnected that nearly every expressed gene exerts a tiny “peripheral” effect, funnelled through fewer “core” genes — this is why PRS (W3) works.

Allele frequency × effect size

Common variants tend to have small effects; large-effect variants tend to be rare (purifying selection removes common, large-effect, deleterious variants) [Timpson 2017].

 effect │ rare, large effect
  size  │  •           (Mendelian-like)
        │     • •
        │        • • •
        │             • • • • •   common, small effect
        │                       • • • • •  (typical GWAS hits)
        └──────────────────────────────────── MAF
  • Sample size is destiny — schizophrenia: ~0 hits at n≈hundreds, 113 loci at n in tens of thousands
  • Effect size ≠ druggability — common HMGCR SNP explains ~0.26% of LDL variance, yet statins are transformative
Important

Architecture can’t be predicted from heritability alone. Choose your study design after you understand the likely architecture.

Study design & QC

GWAS study design

Participants
├── Cases    (n ≥ 5,000)    patients with the disease
└── Controls (n ≥ 10,000)   ancestry-matched, disease-free
          ↓
Genotyping array  →  imputation to a reference panel
          ↓
Quality control (samples + variants)
          ↓
Per-variant association test (+ covariates)
          ↓
Summary statistics → Manhattan / QQ → post-GWAS
Note

Sample size is everything. Early GWAS (n≈2,000) found almost nothing; biobank GWAS (n>500K) find hundreds of loci. Most “failed” early studies were just underpowered for a polygenic architecture.

Quality control

QC step Threshold Why
Sample call rate > 95–98% poor DNA / failed samples
SNP call rate > 99% unreliable genotyping
Hardy–Weinberg eq. p > 1×10⁻⁶ (controls) genotyping error
Minor allele freq. > 1% underpowered for rarer variants
Heterozygosity ±3 SD contamination / inbreeding
Relatedness (kinship) π̂ < 0.125 inflated statistics
Imputation INFO/R² > 0.8 unreliable dosages
Stratification PCA biggest confounder

Population stratification

If cases & controls differ in ancestry, any ancestry-associated variant looks like a disease hit.

▶️ Fix: PCA on genotypes → include top PCs as covariates so ancestry is absorbed by the model.

glm(disease ~ SNP +
      PC1 + PC2 + PC3 + PC4 + PC5 +  # ancestry
      age + sex + batch,             # nuisance
    family = binomial)
ImportantAlways report ancestry — and its trade-off

Mixing populations uncorrected → false positives. Restricting to one ancestry → cleaner stats but limited generalizability (see Diversity).

Reading GWAS results

The Manhattan plot

library(qqman)

manhattan(gwas_results,
          chr = "CHR", bp = "BP", p = "P", snp = "SNP",
          col = c("#185FA5", "#1D9E75"),
          suggestiveline = -log10(1e-5),   # dashed
          genomewideline = -log10(5e-8),   # solid
          highlight = lead_snps,
          main = "GWAS — Type 2 Diabetes (n = 150,000)")

Each point = a variant; x = position, y = −log₁₀(p). “Skyscrapers” are associated loci.

Why the threshold is 5×10⁻⁸

  • ~1 million independent common-variant tests after LD pruning
  • Bonferroni: 0.05 / 1,000,000 = 5×10⁻⁸ → genome-wide significant
  • p < 1×10⁻⁵ → conventional suggestive line
Note

This is calibrated for common SNPs. Rare-variant and structural-variant tests (see Beyond SNPs) need their own thresholds.

QQ plot & genomic inflation (λ)

qq(gwas_results$P, main = "QQ — observed vs expected −log10(p)")

chisq  <- qchisq(gwas_results$P, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
lambda <- median(chisq) / qchisq(0.5, df = 1)
cat("Genomic inflation λ =", round(lambda, 3), "\n")
  • Well-calibrated: hug the diagonal, lift off at the tail (true signal)
  • Inflated (λ > 1.05): all above diagonal → uncorrected stratification / relatedness
  • Deflated (λ < 0.95): over-conservative QC → lost power
  • At very large n, modest λ can be genuine polygenicity — LD-score regression separates the two

Beyond SNPs

Variation that arrays miss

For some traits, common-SNP GWAS nears signal saturation — the next frontier is variation arrays capture poorly [Harris 2025].

Variant class What it is Clinical relevance
CNV del/dup, kb–Mb dosage effects; under-tested
Structural inversions, translocations disrupt genes / distal regulation
Tandem repeats variable repeat counts expansions → neuro disorders
HLA / MHC hyper-polymorphic dominates autoimmune signals

Two examples worth remembering

  • UGT2B17 deletion → prostate cancer — alters testosterone metabolism; frequency varies by population → population-specific risk, invisible to SNP-only analysis [Harris 2025]
  • CYP2D6 copy number → drug dosing — deletions vs duplications shift codeine→morphine conversion (poor vs ultra-rapid metabolizers). Pharmacogenetics: the variant changes the right dose
NoteDosage sensitivity & “human knockouts”

Sequencing enables base-pair CNV calling at biobank scale. Aggregating loss-of-function variants (gnomAD LOEUF) builds dosage-sensitivity maps flagging genes intolerant to disruption — directly useful for clinical variant interpretation.

Post-GWAS: from hit to biology

A hit is rarely the cause

A GWAS hit is usually a tag in LD with the real driver.

rs1234567  p = 3×10⁻²⁴            ← lead SNP (reported)
   ├── rs1234568  r² = 0.98
   ├── rs1234591  r² = 0.95       ← one (or more) is causal
   └── rs1234612  r² = 0.91
   (inherited together in a haplotype block)

Post-GWAS pipeline: 1) Fine-mapping → 2) Functional annotation → 3) Variant→gene → 4) Causal inference

Step 0 — Linkage disequilibrium

LD both enables GWAS (one tag stands in for many) and complicates it (can’t tell tag from cause by p alone).

library(LDlinkR)

ld_matrix <- LDmatrix(
  snps  = c("rs1234567", "rs1234568", "rs1234591"),
  pop   = "CEU",            # 1000 Genomes population
  r2d   = "r2",
  token = "your_token"      # free at ldlink.nci.nih.gov
)

LDproxy(snp = "rs1234567", pop = "CEU", r2d = "r2", token = "your_token")
Warning

The LD reference panel must match your sample’s ancestry — a CEU panel on an East Asian cohort corrupts fine-mapping [Schaid 2018].

Step 1 — Fine-mapping

Modern fine-mapping is Bayesian: compute a posterior inclusion probability (PIP) per variant, then a credible set — the smallest set containing the causal variant(s) with (e.g.) 95% probability [Schaid 2018].

library(susieR)

# SuSiE = Sum of Single Effects — allows multiple causal signals
susie_fit <- susie(X = genotype_matrix, y = phenotype_vector, L = 10)

cs  <- susie_get_cs(susie_fit, coverage = 0.95)  # 95% credible set(s)
pip <- susie_get_pip(susie_fit)                  # per-variant PIP
Note

Fine-mapping shrinks ~200 correlated SNPs to a credible set of a handful — if the data allow it.

What controls fine-mapping resolution

Expected PIP rises with λ = N·R²/(1−R²) and falls as nearby SNPs get more correlated [Schaid 2018]:

  • Larger N → tighter credible sets (cheapest win)
  • High LD (ρ→1) → causal variants statistically indistinguishable in one sample
  • Functional annotation as a prior → modest help (90% set ~17.5 → ~13.5 SNPs for lipids); matters most in weak, high-LD regions
TipRobustness checklist
  • PIPs spread across many SNPs? → you likely can’t resolve one variant here
  • LD reference matches the sample? (compare allele frequencies)
  • Do SuSiE / FINEMAP / PAINTOR agree?
  • Multi-ancestry: assume shared causal variants, allow different effect sizes

Step 2 — Functional annotation

Location Likely mechanism
Coding (missense/nonsense) direct protein change
Splice site altered mRNA / isoform
Promoter / 5′UTR transcription regulation
Enhancer distal gene regulation
Intergenic / intronic unknown — needs eQTL / chromatin
Important

~90% of GWAS hits are non-coding, enriched in regulatory elements and eQTLs — which is exactly why epigenomics (W4–W5) is essential for interpretation.

Step 3 — Variant → gene: colocalization

An eQTL affects a gene’s expression. Colocalization tests whether the GWAS and eQTL signals share the same causal variant.

library(coloc)

coloc_result <- coloc.abf(
  dataset1 = list(pvalues = gwas_pvals, N = 150000, type = "cc", s = 0.3),
  dataset2 = list(pvalues = eqtl_pvals, N = 500,    type = "quant")
)
coloc_result$summary   # PP.H4 = share one causal variant
Tip

PP.H4 > 0.8 → strong evidence the variant acts through that gene → strong effector candidate.

WarningWatch direction of effect (coherence)

A risk allele can down-regulate a gene that looks up-regulated in patients (“incoherence”) — often an impaired protective response. Direction decides agonist vs antagonist [Reay & Cairns 2021].

Step 3 (cont.) — which cell type?

Colocalization names a gene; it doesn’t say which cell. Frameworks like sc-linker integrate scRNA-seq with GWAS via stratified LD-score regression (S-LDSC) [Minton 2022]:

  • Recovered known biology (T cells in eczema; microglia in Alzheimer’s & MS)
  • Surfaced candidates (GABAergic neurons in depression — current drugs target serotonin)
  • Separated disease-state programmes (M cells in ulcerative colitis) from healthy-state

A locus needs both a gene (coloc) and a cell type/state (single-cell) before you claim a mechanism.

Step 4 — Mendelian randomization

Does elevated LDL cause CAD, or just correlate?

Variants = instruments; randomized at conception → mimic a lifelong RCT, immune to lifestyle/SES confounding.

Genetic variants → LDL level → CAD
   (instrument)    (exposure)  (outcome)
library(TwoSampleMR)

exposure_dat <- extract_instruments("ieu-a-300")            # LDL
outcome_dat  <- extract_outcome_data(snps = exposure_dat$SNP,
                                     outcomes = "ieu-a-7")  # CAD
dat    <- harmonise_data(exposure_dat, outcome_dat)
result <- mr(dat)                                            # IVW + sensitivity
Warning

IV assumptions: (1) relevance, (2) independence of confounders, (3) exclusion restriction. #3 is broken by pleiotropy — always run MR-Egger / weighted median [Reay & Cairns 2021].

GWAS for drug repurposing

Existing drugs sit on GWAS signals

Human genetic evidence ~doubles clinical success, so loci are mined for targets [Reay & Cairns 2021].

Trait Gene Drug / class
Schizophrenia DRD2 antipsychotics
Type 2 diabetes PPARG thiazolidinediones
Breast cancer ESR1 tamoxifen
Bone mineral density RANKL denosumab
Rheumatoid arthritis IL6R tocilizumab
Psoriasis IL23R ustekinumab
LDL cholesterol HMGCR statins
Atrial fibrillation SCN5A class-1a antiarrhythmics
Note

A SNP near a gene doesn’t prove the gene is causal — follow-up required.

Three genetic strategies for repurposing

  • Locus → target — Open Targets Genetics, Priority index, MAGMA, TWAS (FUSION, S-PrediXcan)
  • MR for target validation — cis-variants in a druggable gene as instrument (PCSK9, IL6R)
  • Direction of effect — decides agonist vs antagonist (ties back to coherence)

PheWAS: flip the question

One variant, many phenotypes

GWAS   : one disease  → scan all variants    → "which variants?"
PheWAS : one variant  → scan all phenotypes   → "what else does it do?"

Typically run over electronic health records (ICD/CPT codes as phenotypes) [Denny 2016].

  • Pleiotropy mapping — repurposing leads and predictable side-effects
  • EHR-scale — one biobank → thousands of tests at once
  • Pharmacogenomic PheWAS (“MedWAS”) — variant → drug response / adverse events (free-text extraction is the bottleneck)

Diversity: one ancestry is not enough

Why diverse cohorts matter

Most GWAS (→ fine-mapping → PRS) are European-ancestry — a scientific and equity problem [Wojcik 2019].

  • Missed discovery — variants rare/absent in Europeans are invisible; multi-ethnic PAGE found new associations
  • Better fine-mapping — different LD patterns break haplotype blocks → smaller credible sets
  • Poor portability — effect sizes & risk scores don’t transfer → biased clinical use widens disparities
ImportantFor Korean cohorts

Use Korean / East-Asian resources (KoGES, Korea Biobank Array “KCHIP”, TOPMed). Check your base GWAS ancestry matches your target before trusting an association, credible set, or PRS.

Hands-on

Dataset: T2D summary statistics

Public T2D GWAS summary stats (e.g. Mahajan et al. 2022, Nat Genet) — one row per variant, no individual genotypes, hence shareable.

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(qqman)

gwas <- read_tsv(here("data", "raw", "t2d_gwas_summary.tsv"))
glimpse(gwas)
# CHR, BP, SNP, A1, A2, FREQ, BETA, SE, P, N, INFO

Step 1 — QC on summary stats

gwas_clean <- gwas |>
  filter(!is.na(P), P > 0, P <= 1,
         FREQ > 0.01, FREQ < 0.99,   # common variants
         INFO > 0.8) |>              # imputation quality
  mutate(CHR = as.integer(CHR),
         neglogP = -log10(P))

cat("SNPs before QC:", nrow(gwas), "\n")
cat("SNPs after  QC:", nrow(gwas_clean), "\n")

Step 2 — QQ plot & λ

chisq  <- qchisq(gwas_clean$P, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
lambda <- median(chisq) / qchisq(0.5, df = 1)
cat("Lambda (GC) =", round(lambda, 4), "\n")

qq(gwas_clean$P,
   main = paste0("QQ — T2D GWAS  (λ = ", round(lambda, 3), ")"),
   col  = "#185FA5")

Step 3 — Manhattan plot

sig_snps <- gwas_clean |> filter(P < 5e-8) |> arrange(P)
cat("Genome-wide significant variants:", nrow(sig_snps), "\n")

manhattan(gwas_clean,
          chr = "CHR", bp = "BP", p = "P", snp = "SNP",
          col = c("#185FA5", "#1D9E75"),
          suggestiveline = -log10(1e-5),
          genomewideline = -log10(5e-8),
          highlight      = head(sig_snps$SNP, 10),
          main           = "T2D GWAS — Manhattan plot")

Step 4 — Annotate top hits

library(biomaRt)

mart     <- useMart("ensembl", dataset = "hsapiens_gene_ensembl")
top_hits <- sig_snps |> slice_min(P, n = 20)

annotations <- getBM(
  attributes = c("chromosome_name", "start_position",
                 "end_position", "external_gene_name"),
  filters    = "chromosomal_region",
  values     = paste0(top_hits$CHR, ":",
                      top_hits$BP - 5e5, ":", top_hits$BP + 5e5),
  mart       = mart
)
head(annotations)

Step 5 — Regional (locus-zoom) plot

library(gassocplot)

# TCF7L2 — most replicated T2D locus
tcf7l2 <- gwas_clean |>
  filter(CHR == 10, BP >= 114700000, BP <= 115000000)

stack_assoc_plot(
  markers = tcf7l2[, c("SNP", "CHR", "BP")],
  z       = tcf7l2$neglogP,
  corr    = ld_matrix_tcf7l2,   # from LDlinkR, ancestry-matched
  traits  = "T2D",
  ylab    = "-log10(p)"
)

Interrogating any locus

  1. Replicated? in an independent cohort?
  2. LD structure? how big is the credible set?
  3. Functional context? coding, regulatory, eQTL?
  4. Which gene & cell type? nearest ≠ causal
  5. Effect size & direction? small; direction guides drug strategy
  6. Druggable? known/tractable target?

Wrap-up

What GWAS cannot tell you

  • Causality alone — association ≠ causation (MR helps, with assumptions)
  • Rare variants — common-SNP GWAS misses MAF < 1% (need WES/WGS)
  • Non-SNP variation — CNV/SV/repeats need dedicated methods
  • Mechanism alone — an enhancer hit says “something regulates something”
  • Transferability — Euro-centric results may not generalize
  • Gene × environment — static associations miss dynamic biology

GWAS is the beginning of the story, not the end — which is why the rest of the course exists.

Where this connects

GWAS hit identified
   ├─ W3       PRS            → genome-wide risk prediction
   ├─ W4–W5    Epigenomics    → active enhancer?
   ├─ W6–W7    Metagenomics   → microbiome mediation?
   ├─ W8–W9    scRNA-seq      → which cell type?
   ├─ W10      Spatial        → where in tissue?
   ├─ W11      Multi-omics    → convergent evidence
   └─ W12      Drug target    → druggable?
